column1: # Where each note in lex-la.tsv was checked.
# lemma | pos | tgt | note | sources
# A note is the sentence printed under a woven Latin word: in the tooltip,
# joined to the descent sentence on /latin/<word>, in the note column of the
# descent hub, and — when it says "means" or "literally" — as the word's line
# in the discoveries feed. It is a published claim, and until 2026-10-02
# nothing recorded that any of the 28 had been looked up. The first row of the
# pack said so by itself: man → vir, "third-person plural “virī” also means
# “men” collectively". A noun has no person.
# On 2026-10-02 all 28 were read against Lewis & Short for every Latin word a
# note uses, Allen & Greenough for the two that state a rule of grammar, and
# etymonline for every English word a note explains. Five did not stand as
# written and are listed at the foot of this file with what the dictionary
# says, so that nobody restores one in good faith.
# The line repeats the note. That is the point: reword a note and it has no
# source until somebody opens the dictionary again and says which entry.
# The sources field
# Each line names the entries it was checked against, separated by spaces:
#   ls:<key>           Lewis & Short, A Latin Dictionary (1879), by the entry's
#                      key in the Perseus text — os1 is mouth, os2 is bone:
#                      perseus.tufts.edu/hopper/text?doc=Perseus:text:1999.04.0059:entry=<key>
#   ag:<section>       Allen & Greenough's New Latin Grammar (1903), by section:
#                      perseus.tufts.edu/hopper/text?doc=Perseus:text:1999.04.0001:smythp=<section>
#   etym:<english>     https://www.etymonline.com/word/<english>
#   wikt:la:<latin>    https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/<latin>#Latin
#   wikt:en:<english>  https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/<english>#English
# tests/tools/la-notes.test.ts requires every note in lex-la.tsv to have a
# line here repeating it, every line to cite Lewis & Short's entry for the
# note's own headword, and a note that names its row's English etymon to cite
# that word's etymonline entry. It cannot tell an entry somebody read from one
# somebody typed: cite the ones actually opened.
# What a note is held to
# A source that contradicts it, hedges what it states flatly, or says less
# than it does, and the note is rewritten to what the entry says. A loose
# paraphrase of an entry stands: "in Latin it includes the household slaves"
# is weaker than Lewis & Short, for whom familia is first of all "the slaves in
# a household", and it is true.
# The etymon column of lex-la.tsv is not covered here. It wants a ledger of
# its own, and TODO.md has the item.

column1: # Rewritten on 2026-10-02: the old note, and what the dictionary says
#   man     vir      "third-person plural “virī” also means “men” collectively"
#                    virī is the nominative plural of a second-declension noun, and person is
#                    a verb's. ls:vir: "a male person, a man (opp. femina)"; "a husband,
#                    maritus (very freq.)"; human beings only "poet." ls:homo: "a human being,
#                    man".
#   key     clāvis   "the collarbone was named for its key-like shape"
#                    etym:clavicle: "So called supposedly from its function as the 'fastener'
#                    of the shoulder", the sense "a loan-translation of Greek kleis", and the
#                    bone "Medieval Latin clavicula", used c. 980. ls:clavicula has "A small
#                    key", a tendril and "a bar, bolt of the door" — no bone and no shape, which
#                    is why the note says medieval.
#   cow     vacca    "Jenner named the vaccine after the cowpox he used"
#                    etym:vaccination: the word Jenner used "for the technique he publicized",
#                    from vaccine (adj.), 1798; etym:vaccine: the noun is 1846, "from French
#                    vaccin". wikt:en:vaccine: what Jenner coined was variolae vaccinae, his
#                    name for cowpox. Nobody says he named the vaccine.
#   shadow  umbra    "a little shade"
#                    That is umbella — ls:umbella: "dim. umbra (a little shadow, i. e. meton.),
#                    a sunshade, parasol" — and through it umbrella. The tooltip prints a note
#                    whether or not the etymon badge is on, and alone under umbra this one read
#                    as a gloss of umbra, which is shade and not little.
#   yes     ita      "classical Latin has no bare word for yes; “ita” means “thus”"
#                    ag:336: "There is no one Latin word in common use meaning simply yes or
#                    no" — the note had dropped "in common use". ls:ita: "In affirmations, esp.
#                    in replies, yes, it is so, just so, true".
